title: “Laredo families deserve to know”: Mayor Treviño questions border buoy risks
excerpt: Mayor Victor Treviño is asking federal officials to meet in Laredo and explain the risks of the border buoys that washed down the Rio Grande to Laredo in July flooding.
content:
Mayor Victor Treviño wants answers about the border buoys sitting in Laredo's stretch of the Rio Grande — and he wants federal officials to come to Laredo to give them. The mayor raised his concerns at a news conference Monday afternoon at City Hall, according to the Laredo Morning Times.

The buoys are floating barriers installed on the Rio Grande to deter crossings along the U.S.-Mexico border. They were not originally placed in Laredo. But during July flooding, 70 to 120 of them were dislodged and traveled down the river from El Paso to Laredo, where they now present a challenge for the city.

Treviño said he has been concerned for some time about what the buoys mean for the river, and he pointed to the July incident as proof of how unpredictable the Rio Grande can be during heavy rain. His concerns include the risk of flooding in Laredo when the river rises, the buoys' long-term effects on water flow and water quality, and whether Laredo families could lose access to the water the community depends on. The potential effects, he said, are still largely unknown.

The city has reached out to federal officials asking them to meet in Laredo, and Treviño asked for a meeting, a site visit and more information about the project's plans and potential effects. “We're requesting a meeting, a site visit and more information about the plans and potential effects. Laredo should have a seat at the table when decisions are being made about our border,” he said. He added that the city has heard very little about the risks, the monitoring plans, or who would be responsible if something goes wrong — a lack of information he called unacceptable.

Treviño stressed that his questions are not a challenge to border security itself. “We understand the need for border security, and we're not asking anyone to stop doing their job,” he said. “But any effort of this size should come with clear answers and a chance for our community to understand what's being done on our river.”

No specific federal agency was named in the report, and no federal response has been reported. The city is still waiting for federal officials to agree to meet in Laredo and provide the information Treviño requested.

Update — November 13, 2026

After heavy rainfall this week, buoys in the Rio Grande near Webb County came loose again — the second time since July — and Mayor Victor Treviño called for the loose buoys to be recovered and for a pause on further placement, KGNS reported on November 11. KGNS cameras captured loose buoys in the river, and the mayor said they landed on the Mexican side of the river, where water intakes are more exposed. U.S. Customs and Border Protection told KGNS it has placed 14 miles of a planned 122 miles of “waterborne barriers” in the Laredo sector. The mayor said the buoys were placed again after the July incident without the studies he had requested, and he repeated his call for federal officials to meet in Laredo. Residents of the Azteca neighborhood also told KGNS they worry a border wall could be built through their neighborhood; the mayor said Laredo has avoided a border wall through negotiation and collaboration and that he plans to keep presenting evidence to prevent wall construction in the Azteca area.

Source: Laredo Morning Times (lmtonline.com). KGNS — “Loose buoys prompt Laredo mayor’s call for pause; residents raise wall concerns” (Nov. 11, 2026).
